newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo eyes Lon club deal by the end of 1997-Djunic.
newsitem.headline: Yugo eyes Lon club deal by the end of 1997-Djunic.

text.p: Yugoslavia hopes to clinch a deal with commercial creditors by the end of 1997 but will start paying back only after rejoining the International Monetary Fund (IMF), a senior government official said on Tuesday.

"We have struck no deal yet, but have opened a process and hope to have a deal by the end of the year. But any debt repayment will begin only when Yugoslavia returns to the IMF," Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic, in charge of reforms, said at a luncheon with journalists.
Relations with the IMF are at a low point because of concerns in the West over what is seen as Belgrade's reluctance to fully implement the Dayton peace agreements.
Speaking as he returned from London talks with commercial creditors, Djunic said Yugoslavia was also preparing for future talks with the Paris Club of government creditors.
He said any deal with them would also have to follow readmission to the IMF and the World Bank.

Yugoslav debt to the Paris club creditors is unofficially estimated at $3.6 billion. Debt to the IMF and the World Bank stands at $1.6 billion and to other financial institutions at $1.2 billion. Belgrade owes $2 billion for debt rescheduling costs and interest on arrears.

Belgrade asked last week for an 80 percent debt write-off and offered to pay back up to $500 million out of $2.4 billion debt through a 25-year syndicated loan with a nine-year grace period and an interest starting from an annual 3.00 percent and progressing to LIBOR plus 13/18.
It also asked creditors to accept $1.7 billion in principle and $700 million in interest.
"Our proposal was not aggressive because it was their request that we come to London with a concrete proposal."

"We have proposed a loan as an instrument, although we know Brady or bullet bonds are more acceptable to the market, for being more liquid and having no limits. But we think a loan would have advantages for it can be controlled," he added.
Creditors were shown alternative forecasts for growth rates, exports and the current account, based on realistic, conservative economic forecasts, not on expected foreign capital inflow, he said.
"The whole study is based on our cash-flow expectations
by 2010, which we think can endure a debt servicing burden. We also think a realistic scenario is for a six percent GDP growth in real terms. Anything above would be inconsistent," he said.
The deputy prime minister said a deal with Yugoslavia will help creditors collect around 75 percent of the debt.

"Investors have already collected 61 cents for each dollar after deals with Slovenia and Croatia. Now they get two more cents with the Bosnian deal and with Yugoslavia they would get another 10-12 cents. This means they get 75 cents per dollar, which they could not get from any other East European country."
He also said there were no intentions to exclude related parties from the deal, although Serbian and Montenegrin related parties were squeezed from deals with Croatia and Slovenia.
"Exclusion of related parties would be against market principles which treat each debt holder equally," Djunic said. Around $1 billion of the $2.4 billion is estimated to be held by related parties.

"We have also made it very clear that any talks, figures and deals cannot be conditioned with succession issues and division of assets of former Yugoslavia," Djunic said. He said some $10 billion in former Yugoslavia's reserves disappeared after the country broke up.
Former Yugoslavia's central bank was based in Belgrade but operated through eight republican and provincial affiliates, which in practice acted independently and manipulated with reserves.
"The question is how other Yugoslav republics managed to build up their hard currency reserves in such a short time after experiencing dramatic economic declines," he said.
